title: Blood, Life and One Altar
overview: This chapter requires all sacrifices to be brought to the one place of worship and forbids eating blood, because blood was seen as the life of a creature.

parts.label: Killing animals outside the tent (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Anyone who killed an ox, lamb or goat without bringing it to the tent of meeting, the portable worship tent, was counted guilty of bloodshed, as if they had taken a life wrongly. They were to be "cut off" from the people, a penalty scholars are unsure about; it may mean death, banishment, or judgment left to God.

parts.label: No more goat idols (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: People had been sacrificing in open fields, some of them to goat idols, likely desert spirits pictured as goats, and the text calls this unfaithfulness, like cheating on a spouse. Bringing every offering to the priest at one altar, a rule for foreigners living among Israel too, kept worship focused on the LORD alone.

parts.label: Blood is life (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: Eating blood was forbidden because blood was seen as the animal's life, which belonged to God and was used only on the altar to make atonement, meaning to cover wrongdoing and restore the relationship. Christians later read this in light of Jesus, seeing his death as the blood that makes atonement once for all.

parts.label: Covering a hunted animal's blood (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: Even wild game had to have its blood drained and covered with earth, and the reason given is that a creature's life is its blood. Many think the rule also stopped people from using the blood in religious rituals, such as pouring it out to gods of the hunt, though that is an educated guess.

parts.label: Animals found dead (vv. 15-16)
parts.note: Eating an animal that died on its own or was killed by wild beasts made a person ritually unclean, unfit for worship for a time, probably because its blood had not been drained. Washing and waiting until evening restored them, but anyone who skipped the washing remained answerable for it.

disagreement: Interpreters differ on whether verses 3 and 4 required every animal killed even for food to be brought to the altar during the wilderness years, or only animals meant as sacrifices, since Deuteronomy 12 later allows killing animals at home.
think: What would change if the taking of an animal's life were treated as a serious act rather than an ordinary one?
